sources.claim: C++ if, switch, and conditional expressions choose paths from contextually converted conditions, with initialization statements able to scope decision state.

canonicalExplanation.summary: C++ `if` and `switch` work like C's, with useful extras. An **if with an initialiser**, `if (auto r = parse(text); r) { ... } else { ... }`, declares a variable that exists **only inside that if/else**, keeping temporary decision state from leaking into the rest of the function. `switch` still **falls through** to the next case unless you `break`; mark deliberate fall-through with `[[fallthrough]];`. Switching over an `enum class` without a `default` lets `-Wswitch` warn when a new value isn't handled. And as always, **test every boundary**.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner parses user input into `auto result` near the top of a long function, checks it in an if, and then, 40 lines later, accidentally reuses the stale result for a different input. Their menu switch also runs two actions for one choice. An if initializer parses a value and keeps the parse result scoped to the success and failure branches. In this lesson you'll write and test boundary-complete selection logic.

```predict
{"question": "In `if (auto n = parse(s); n) { ... } else { ... }`, can code after the whole if/else use n?", "options": ["Yes", "No: n exists only in the if and else branches"], "answer": 1, "why": "Narrow scope means no stale reuse later."}
```

sections.heading: The rule: scope decision state, break every case
Boundaries

includes: Use if initialisers to scope decision state to the branches that need it.
Write switches with break or [[fallthrough]], enum class coverage, and boundary tests.

outcomes: Write and test boundary-complete selection logic.

examples.title: Parsing a number inside the if
examples.situation: An if initializer parses a value and keeps the parse result scoped to the success and failure branches.
walkthrough: **An if initializer parses a value:** if (auto n = parse_int(input); n).
**Keeps the parse result scoped to the success and failure branches:** n is usable in both, gone afterwards.
**No stale reuse:** code 40 lines later can't touch n, so the next input will get its own fresh parse.
examples.result: Each decision uses its own fresh result, and the stale-value bug can't happen.

examples.title: The menu that did two things
examples.situation: Choice Add also printed "remove" because its case lacked break.
walkthrough: Add break to every case, or [[fallthrough]] where intended.
examples.result: Each choice runs exactly one action.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Every switch label ends its branch automatically in C++ unless braces are omitted.
misconceptions.correction: Braces don't stop fall-through; only break, return or another jump does. Without them, execution continues into the next case.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "The menu that did two things", why did Add also print remove?

analogy.example: An if initialiser is like **a sticky note you write at a decision point and throw away once you've decided**. Nobody finds an old note later and acts on it by mistake. A switch without break is **a set of dominoes**: knock one and the rest fall unless you place a stopper (break).
limitations: Real notes can be kept; scoped variables really vanish.
[[fallthrough]] is a sign saying "these dominoes should fall".

steps.explanation: An if initializer parses a value right at the decision.
The parse result is scoped to the success and failure branches.

trace.textAlternative: Tracing an if initialiser. Step 1, Init: n is optional(42). An if initializer parses a value right at the decision. Step 2, Branch: output is got 42. The parse result is scoped to the success and failure branches. Step 3, After: n is out of scope. Later code cannot reuse the stale parse result.

nearTransfer.prompt: Write std::string shipping(double total) returning "none" below 20, "standard" from 20 to under 50, and "free" from 50. Test 19.99, 20, 49.99, 50 and a negative total.

farTransfer.prompt: Add Choice::Help to the enum and compile: read the -Wswitch warning, handle it, then add a menu loop using an if initialiser to parse each line of input and switch on the result. Test invalid input and every choice.
expectedEvidence: Every choice and invalid input tested.

remediation.explanation: For each decision ask: **does any variable outlive the decision it served?** Scope it with an initialiser. For each case: **break or [[fallthrough]]?** Then test the boundaries.
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "The menu that did two things".

recap.summary: To write boundary-complete selection logic, scope decision state with if initialisers, end each switch case with break or mark [[fallthrough]], switch over enum class without default so the compiler checks coverage, and test values on both sides of every boundary.
